other_side: NLW's lead is that models are now capable enough, the missing ingredient is context, and the sensible response is an audit that hands recurring work over. Zitron's nearest published argument attacks the arithmetic underneath that audit: he says nobody can measure the return on AI, or even "create a standard measurement of the cost of a task", because outputs are hallucination-prone and every harness behaves differently. His evidence is billing rather than benchmarks — GitHub Copilot users burning a third of a month's credits in a few hours once token pricing arrived, Uber's COO saying the spend was getting harder to justify, Walmart and Amazon telling staff to stop using AI for its own sake. And on the point NLW calls checkability, Zitron's position is that the vigilance never ends: a model with no ability to learn outside training can go wrong unpredictably on any given run, so the human stays in the loop indefinitely.
truth_beneath: Both men orbit one variable: the cost of checking work you have handed over, and whether that cost falls as the machine learns how you work. They agree on more than the framing admits — that most delegable work is dull and recurring, that output must be verified, and that users have been shielded from what a task really costs. The empirical question is whether verification and cost per task fall as observed context accumulates; the observable that settles it is organisations publishing before-and-after error rates and per-task spend on a specific deputized process, rather than adoption anecdotes. The residue is worldview: Whittemore reads a solvable context gap, Zitron an unmeasurable product sold on obscured pricing. Whittemore is vindicated if recurring processes run on spot checks at stable cost; Zitron if checking still takes as long as doing and bills keep surprising people. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is their shared premise that checkability decides everything. Watch for the first honest published per-task cost and error rate on a deputized workflow.
